03 · Process & Explorations

From audit to one header

Process
1
Audit

Every existing header across all capabilities and applications.

2
Talk

The PM and lead developer of each product and capability.

3
Map

Every function each one needs, from common to unique.

4
Iterate

Header options for each capability and product.

5
Converge

Compared them side by side into one header where all needs meet.

Along the way, six directions answered three questions.

QUESTION 01

Where do the details live?

ANSWERDetails stay under the name, one toggle away.
OPTION A
"More" tab
DroppedThe tab sits far from the name it describes.
KeptKey icons only, the rest in the kebab.
OPTION C
Details below, "Less" to close
KeptMetadata rows under the description, collapsible.
QUESTION 02

How compact can it get?

ANSWERTwo rows minimum: the path on top, a big name below.
OPTION D
Title inside the breadcrumb
DroppedThe name loses weight.
OPTION E
Single row
DroppedAlmost no context.
OPTION F
Everything in one bar
DroppedActions drift away from the app name.
QUESTION 03

Where do the actions go?

ANSWERFrequent, safe actions visible. Risky ones in the kebab.
OPTION B
Actions up front
Kept"More info" right beside the description.
DroppedScale and Stop too exposed in the header.

06 · Key Decisions

What I chose, and what it cost

PRIORITY 1 · ALWAYS VISIBLE
Status, name, tag, settings

What every app needs, every visit.

PRIORITY 2 · ONE CLICK
Metadata, job counts, monitoring

Behind the info toggle.

PRIORITY 3 · IN THE KEBAB
Restart, upgrade, scaling, mesh

Rare or risky, varies by app.

Ordered from most to least important, and the visual weight follows the same order. Designers place each app's or capability's items into these zones as needed.

DECISION 01

Collapsed by default

WHYThe work below matters more than metadata.
COSTDetails are one click away.
DECISION 02

Status before the name

WHYHealth and identity in one glance.
COSTOne dot carries a lot of meaning.
DECISION 03

Risky actions in overflow

WHYRestart and upgrade, away from stray clicks.
COSTRare actions sit one level deeper.
DECISION 04

Edit in place

WHYSmall edits should not open a modal.
COSTOnly for short, single-field edits.
DECISION 05

Built for what comes next

WHYNew capabilities keep arriving, and we cannot know their actions yet. Every priority zone has room, so anything new already has a place.
COSTEach new item has to be ranked before it is placed.

08 · Edge Cases

When the content misbehaves

LONG NAMES
Breadcrumbs truncate, full name on hover
ERROR STATE
Status dot turns red, beside the name
EMPTY
"No tags assigned" with Add tag ready
ZERO COUNTS
Jobs at 0 still show, so empty reads as good
09 · Component Model

Composed from functions

The anatomy maps one-to-one to the code.

<AppHeader state={collapsed | expanded}>
├─ <ContextBar> // RegionSelector · HelpMenu · UserMenu
├─ <Breadcrumb /> // text links with chevrons
├─ <TitleRow> // StatusDot · EditableTitle · Actions
├─ <DescriptionRow> // InfoToggle · EditableText
└─ <MetadataPanel visible={isExpanded}>
├─ <MetaField /> // instance · version · space · profile
├─ <JobStatusGroup /> // created · running · faulted…
└─ <ToggleGroup /> // monitor · instrumentation
10 · Outcome

What changed

44%

Shorter when collapsed, handed back to the work.

Expanded222px
Collapsed125px
10+

Apps and capabilities served by one header.

3

Priority tiers that any new app slots into.

Reviewed and approved by the Head of Design, product and engineering stakeholders.
REFLECTION

On a platform, the header is on every screen, so every pixel is paid again and again. Designing it as priority zones, not fixed content, means it can grow with apps we have not seen yet.
